title: Mould and mushrooms (fungi)
keyIdea: Mushrooms, toadstools and mould are living things called fungi. One of them is a fungus. Fungi are not plants: they have no green leaves and do not make food from sunlight. They feed on old food, rotting wood and dead leaves, and break them down into soil. Mould grows from tiny spores that float in the air. Some wild mushrooms are poison, so look but never eat one you find.

kid: Leave some bread out for a week. Soon you see fuzzy spots. They are green, white or blue. The spots get bigger each day. That is mould. Mould is alive. It grows!
Mould is a fungus. Mushrooms and toadstools are fungi too. Fungi are not plants. They have no green leaves. They do not need light to make food.
Fungi eat old and dead things. They grow on old fruit, rotting logs and dead leaves. Bit by bit, the dead things break down. They turn into soil. So fungi help tidy up the woods.
Some mushrooms in the park or woods are poison. They can make you very ill. Look with your eyes. Tell a grown-up. Never eat a wild mushroom. Do not eat food with mould on it.
adult: Fungi are their own kingdom of living things, separate from plants and animals. Unlike plants, they have no chlorophyll and cannot make food by photosynthesis. They release enzymes onto dead material and absorb the nutrients, which is why they are called decomposers. Mushrooms and toadstools are the fruiting bodies of a much larger network of threads underground. Yeast, used to make bread rise, is a fungus too.

This topic is not a named statutory objective at ages 5 to 7, but it builds directly on them. England's Year 1 and Year 2 science asks children to tell apart things that are living, dead and never alive, and to explore micro-habitats such as under logs and leaf litter. It prepares for later work on decomposers (NGSS 5-LS2-1) and on sorting living things into broad groups, including fungi, in Year 6.

Common mistakes: thinking mould is dirt or just the food changing colour, rather than a living thing that grows; calling a mushroom a plant because it grows in the ground; thinking mould appears from nowhere, when it grows from spores, tiny cells that drift in the air; and believing that a mushroom which looks like a shop one is safe to eat. Some wild fungi, such as the death cap, can kill.

In the lab your child watches mould spots grow on bread over a week, sorts fungi from plants, taps the places where fungi grow, drags a fungus onto a dead leaf, a log and an apple core to watch them break down into soil, and sorts what is safe to do when they find a wild mushroom.

familyTip: Put a slice of bread in a sealed clear bag with a few drops of water and look at it each day for a week, without opening it. Count the spots together. Then throw the bag away unopened. On a walk, look for mushrooms on logs and in leaves, but do not touch or pick them.

visual.caption: Is it a fungus or a plant? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: watch mould grow on bread, sort fungi from plants, find where fungi grow, watch fungi turn dead things into soil.

practice.prompt: Fuzzy green spots grow on old bread. What are they?
practice.hint: The spots get bigger every day. Does dirt grow?
practice.explain: The spots are mould. Mould is a fungus. It is alive, so it grows and spreads.

practice.prompt: On the grass there are {a} mushrooms and {b} daisies. How many are fungi?
practice.hint: Daisies are plants. Count only the mushrooms.
practice.explain: Only the mushrooms are fungi. Daisies are plants. So {a} are fungi.

practice.prompt: A log has {a} mushrooms on it. In the night, {b} more grow. How many mushrooms now?
practice.hint: Mushrooms are alive, so more can grow. Start at {a} and count on {b}.
practice.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b}. Now there are {=a+b} mushrooms on the log.

practice.prompt: You see a big mushroom in the park. What should you do?
practice.explain: Never eat a wild mushroom. Some are poison and can make you very ill. Look with your eyes and tell a grown-up.

pool.prompt: In the wood there are {a} toadstools and {b} trees. How many are fungi?
pool.hint: Trees are plants. Toadstools are fungi.
pool.explain: Only the toadstools are fungi. Trees are plants. So {a} are fungi.

pool.prompt: A bowl has {a} old oranges with mould and {b} fresh ones. How many have a fungus growing on them?
pool.hint: Mould is a fungus. Which oranges have mould?
pool.explain: The mould is a fungus, and it is only on the old oranges. So {a} oranges have a fungus.

pool.hint: Does a mushroom have green leaves?
pool.explain: A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant. It has no green leaves and does not make food from light.

choices: On an old, damp piece of bread
pool.hint: Mould needs food and a damp place.
pool.explain: Mould feeds on old food and likes it damp. A clean plate and a stone have nothing to feed on.

pool.prompt: What do fungi do to dead leaves?
pool.hint: Think about the log and the leaf in the lab.
pool.explain: Fungi feed on dead leaves and break them down. What is left becomes soil for new plants.

pool.prompt: Ben says mould just comes from nowhere. What is right?
choices: It grows from tiny spores in the air
The baker puts it in the bread
pool.hint: Spores are too small to see, but they float in the air.
pool.explain: Mould grows from tiny spores that float in the air and land on old food. They are too small to see.

pool.hint: One is a plant and one was never alive.
pool.explain: A toadstool is a fungus. A daisy is a plant, and a pebble was never alive.

pool.prompt: Your bread has fuzzy mould on one corner. What should you do?
choices: Scrape it off and eat it
pool.hint: Mould can spread through soft bread where you cannot see it.
pool.explain: Do not eat mouldy bread. The mould can spread inside the bread, even where you cannot see it.
